claim: The skin surface contains very few bacteria as detected by EUB338 FISH probe.
source: We first used EUB338 FISH on biopsied healthy adult human facial tissues and found that the skin surface contains very few bacteria (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1A and quantified in Figure 1D showing low enrichment scores for stratum corneum.

claim: Clusters of bacteria were found within hair follicles and other cutaneous skin structures like comedos.
source: In contrast, clusters of bacteria were found within hair follicles and other cutaneous skin structures like comedos (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1B and quantified in Figure 1D.

claim: EUB338 staining works well in stationary-phase cells of multiple skin microbiome bacterial species (Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Micrococcus luteus, and Corynebacterium striatum).
source: However, we confirmed that EUB338 staining works well in stationary-phase cells of multiple skin microbiome bacterial species (Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Micrococcus luteus, and Corynebacterium striatum) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The median enrichment score for human follicles was 11.24.
source: The median enrichment score for human follicles was 11.24 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The skin surface (stratum corneum) had an enrichment score of just 0.188.
source: In contrast, the skin surface (stratum corneum) had an enrichment score of just 0.188.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: For C. acnes, the enrichment score was 3.14 for follicles compared to 0.67 for the stratum corneum.
source: For C. acnes, the enrichment score was 3.14 for follicles compared to 0.67 for the stratum corneum (Figure 1D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from C. acnes-specific FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: There are some visible bacteria on the skin surface, especially in areas near subsurface structures.
source: We note that while the majority of intact skin-associated bacteria were not associated with the skin surface, there are some visible bacteria on the skin surface, especially in areas near subsurface structures (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Observation from FISH imaging data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Propidium monoazide (PMA) binds irreversibly to double-stranded DNA upon photoactivation to inhibit PCR amplification.
source: To this end, we utilized the cell-impermeable small molecule propidium monoazide (PMA), which binds irreversibly to double-stranded DNA upon photoactivation to inhibit PCR amplification (Figure 2A; Nocker et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from Nocker et al., 2006 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: When PMA photoactivation is performed before the cell lysis step of DNA isolation, the genomic DNA inside viable bacteria is protected from PMA binding because PMA is cell-impermeable, while cell-free DNA or DNA within permeabilized bacteria becomes PMA-bound.
source: When PMA photoactivation is performed before the cell lysis step of DNA isolation, the genomic DNA inside viable bacteria is protected from PMA binding because PMA is cell-impermeable, while cell-free DNA or DNA within permeabilized bacteria becomes PMA-bound.
evidence: Based on the known mechanism of PMA and the experimental design shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PMA-ddPCR viability scores for skin sites ranged between 0.02 and 0.12.
source: PMA-ddPCR revealed that the viability scores for these sites ranged between 0.02 and 0.12 (0 represents a fully nonviable population, 1.0 represents a fully viable population), indicating that the majority of bacterial DNA found on the skin surface are not associated with viable cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of bacterial DNA found on the skin surface are not associated with viable cells.
source: PMA-ddPCR revealed that the viability scores for these sites ranged between 0.02 and 0.12 (0 represents a fully nonviable population, 1.0 represents a fully viable population), indicating that the majority of bacterial DNA found on the skin surface are not associated with viable cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: Inferred from the low viability scores (0.02-0.12) measured by PMA-ddPCR shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In all non-skin microbiome sites, the viability score was significantly higher than for the skin, ranging from 0.4 (saliva) to 0.87 (feces).
source: We found that in all non-skin microbiome sites, the viability score was significantly higher than for the skin, ranging from 0.4 (saliva) to 0.87 (feces) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2C comparing skin and non-skin sites.

claim: The average viability for follicle contents was greater than tenfold higher for follicle contents than for the skin surface.
source: The average viability for follicle contents was greater than tenfold higher for follicle contents than for the skin surface, confirming that cells in hair follicles are more viable than those on the skin surface.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2D comparing follicle contents (viability score 0.15) to forehead swabs (viability score 0.013).

claim: Cells in hair follicles are more viable than those on the skin surface.
source: The average viability for follicle contents was greater than tenfold higher for follicle contents than for the skin surface, confirming that cells in hair follicles are more viable than those on the skin surface.
evidence: Inferred from the tenfold higher viability score for follicle contents compared to skin surface shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The surface of healthy, non-sterilized human skin is sparsely colonized.
source: Together, our results from FISH on biopsies and PMA-ddPCR on skin swabs independently support the conclusion that the skin surface is populated by few viable bacterial cells, indicating that the surface of healthy, non-sterilized human skin is sparsely colonized.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from both FISH data (Figure 1) and PMA-ddPCR data (Figure 2).

claim: At each skin site sampled, compared to traditional sequencing, the PMA-treated samples were less rich and less diverse.
source: These experiments established that at each skin site sampled, compared to traditional sequencing, the PMA-treated samples were less rich (richness, R, is a measure of the number of identifiable bacterial taxa) and less diverse (diversity, H, is measured by the Shannon diversity index) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Samples that had greater richness in traditional sequencing showed proportionally larger decreases in richness and Shannon diversity with PMA-seq.
source: Furthermore, samples that had greater richness in traditional sequencing (Rtrad) showed proportionally larger decreases in richness and Shannon diversity with PMA-seq (RPMA and HPMA) (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of sequencing data shown in Figure 3B and C demonstrating correlation between traditional richness and change in richness/diversity.

claim: Although it appears by traditional sequencing that there is a wide range of richness values at different skin sites (1–30 different taxa), in reality the richness across the skin microbiome at different body sites is relatively similar and low (1–10 different taxa).
source: These results suggest that, although it appears by traditional sequencing that there is a wide range of richness values at different skin sites (1–30 different taxa), in reality the richness across the skin microbiome at different body sites is relatively similar and low (1–10 different taxa).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of traditional sequencing and PMA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The viable skin microbiome tends to be dominated by a relatively small number of taxa at most sites.
source: In fact, our results suggest that the viable skin microbiome tends to be dominated by a relatively small number of taxa at most sites.
evidence: Inferred from the low richness and diversity values observed with PMA-seq shown in Figure 3.

claim: The abundances of most bacterial taxa at any given body site are overestimated by traditional sequencing, as most taxa had PMA index values close to 0.
source: Calculating PMA indices revealed that the abundances of most bacterial taxa at any given body site are overestimated by traditional sequencing, as most taxa had PMA index values close to 0 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of PMA index values shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The four most abundant bacterial families (Propionibacteriaceae, Staphylococcaceae, Corynebacteriaceae, and Micrococcaceae) made up 93% of total sequencing reads (96% of PMA-seq reads and 91% of traditional sequencing reads).
source: The four most abundant bacterial families (Propionibacteriaceae, Staphylococcaceae, Corynebacteriaceae, and Micrococcaceae) made up 93% of total sequencing reads (96% of PMA-seq reads and 91% of traditional sequencing reads) and demonstrated interesting family-level PMA index patterns.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: Traditional sequencing accurately represents Propionibacteriaceae abundance in sebaceous sites (demonstrated by a PMA index close to 0.5), but overrepresents Propionibacteriaceae in moist and dry sites (PMA indices of 0.2–0.3).
source: PMA-seq revealed that traditional sequencing accurately represents Propionibacteriaceae abundance in sebaceous sites (demonstrated by a PMA index close to 0.5), but overrepresents Propionibacteriaceae in moist and dry sites (PMA indices of 0.2–0.3).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of PMA index values for Propionibacteriaceae shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Propionibacteriaceae dominated sebaceous sites (accounting for >75% of all viable bacteria in most sebaceous samples), but did not dominate moist or dry sites (their viable abundance did not exceed 50% of all viable bacteria in any of those samples).
source: Furthermore, Propionibacteriaceae dominated sebaceous sites (accounting for >75% of all viable bacteria in most sebaceous samples), but did not dominate moist or dry sites (their viable abundance did not exceed 50% of all viable bacteria in any of those samples) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of relative abundance data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Traditional sequencing overestimates the abundance of Corynebacteriaceae at every skin site except for the nares.
source: Bacteria in the family Corynebacteriaceae are also considered main constituents of the skin microbiome, but our results showed that traditional sequencing overestimates the abundance of Corynebacteriaceae at every skin site except for the nares.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of PMA index values for Corynebacteriaceae shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Micrococcaceae were overrepresented by traditional sequencing at every site except for the hair shaft.
source: Interestingly, Micrococcaceae were overrepresented by traditional sequencing at every site except for the hair shaft.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of PMA index values for Micrococcaceae shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the hair shaft, Micrococcaceae were abundant by PMA-seq but almost undetectable by traditional sequencing.
source: In the hair shaft, Micrococcaceae were abundant by PMA-seq but almost undetectable by traditional sequencing.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of relative abundance data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most skin sites are colonized by a relatively small number of bacterial families.
source: These results suggest that most skin sites are colonized by a relatively small number of bacterial families, different families distinctly colonize different skin sites, and the majority of the additional bacterial DNA on the skin surface come from inviable bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the PMA-seq data showing low richness and dominance by few families shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Different families distinctly colonize different skin sites.
source: These results suggest that most skin sites are colonized by a relatively small number of bacterial families, different families distinctly colonize different skin sites, and the majority of the additional bacterial DNA on the skin surface come from inviable bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the site-specific patterns of bacterial family abundance shown in Figure 4.

claim: The majority of the additional bacterial DNA on the skin surface come from inviable bacteria.
source: These results suggest that most skin sites are colonized by a relatively small number of bacterial families, different families distinctly colonize different skin sites, and the majority of the additional bacterial DNA on the skin surface come from inviable bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the low viability scores and differences between traditional sequencing and PMA-seq shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: Mouse skin shows a high abundance of bacteria in hair follicles (enrichment score of 15.26) with relatively few bacteria on the skin surface (enrichment score of 0.21).
source: We observed the same bacterial distributions as seen in the human tissues: a high abundance of bacteria in hair follicles (enrichment score of 15.26) with relatively few bacteria on the skin surface (enrichment score of 0.21) (Figure 5A and D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from FISH imaging data on K14-H2B-GFP mouse tissue shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Nude mice skin shows similar bacterial distributions with follicle-associated enrichment score of 10.79 compared to 1.13 for the skin surface.
source: To test how fur impacts the presence of bacteria on the skin surface, we performed FISH staining on skin from nude mice (SKH1-Hrhr Elite) and found similar bacterial distributions (follicle-associated enrichment score of 10.79 compared to 1.13 for the skin surface) (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from FISH imaging data on nude mouse tissue shown in Figure 5B and D.

claim: The low numbers of skin-surface-associated bacteria found in the human tissue samples are not simply a result of pre-biopsy sterilization.
source: Because the mouse tissue was untreated with any sterilizing agents prior to dissection, these results also suggest that the low numbers of skin-surface-associated bacteria found in the human tissue samples are not simply a result of pre-biopsy sterilization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that untreated mouse tissue shows similar patterns to sterilized human tissue.

claim: The PMA-ddPCR-based viability score for mouse skin microbiome sites was similar to the average viability score for human skin sites (0.066 and 0.045, respectively).
source: As further evidence that our previous findings are not human-specific, the PMA-ddPCR-based viability score for mouse skin microbiome sites was similar to the average viability score for human skin sites (0.066 and 0.045, respectively) and was much lower than the viability score for the mouse or human fecal microbiome (0.98 and 0.66, respectively) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PMA-ddPCR data on mouse and human samples shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The viability score for mouse skin was much lower than the viability score for the mouse or human fecal microbiome (0.98 and 0.66, respectively).
source: As further evidence that our previous findings are not human-specific, the PMA-ddPCR-based viability score for mouse skin microbiome sites was similar to the average viability score for human skin sites (0.066 and 0.045, respectively) and was much lower than the viability score for the mouse or human fecal microbiome (0.98 and 0.66, respectively) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Despite having distinct skin biology, both humans and mice have an abundance of bacterial DNA on the skin surface that is not associated with viable cells.
source: These results indicate that, despite having distinct skin biology, both humans and mice have an abundance of bacterial DNA on the skin surface that is not associated with viable cells.
evidence: Inferred from the similar low viability scores observed in both human and mouse skin shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Four of the five volunteers demonstrated significant reduction in the absolute amount of DNA upon sterilization.
source: Focusing on the PMA-untreated samples, we found that four of the five volunteers demonstrated significant reduction in the absolute amount of DNA upon sterilization (Figure 6B), but that the overall bacterial composition of the skin microbiome remained relatively stable (Figure 6A, all bacteria listed in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from ddPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The overall bacterial composition of the skin microbiome remained relatively stable after sterilization.
source: Focusing on the PMA-untreated samples, we found that four of the five volunteers demonstrated significant reduction in the absolute amount of DNA upon sterilization (Figure 6B), but that the overall bacterial composition of the skin microbiome remained relatively stable (Figure 6A, all bacteria listed in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.).
evidence: Qualitative observation from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Over the course of the perturbation-recovery experiment, the communities converged back to the PMA-treated baseline samples.
source: We found that comparing samples with and without the use of PMA to the PMA-treated baseline community resulted in a consistent pattern across all individuals. Over the course of the experiment, the communities converged back to the PMA-treated baseline samples but showed no consistent patterns of similarity relative to the PMA-untreated baseline samples (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of Bray-Curtis dissimilarity shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Bacterial DNA on the skin surface can be readily removed and is continuously replenished by viable bacterial populations in protected reservoirs below the skin surface.
source: This result supports the hypothesis that bacterial DNA on the skin surface can be readily removed and is continuously replenished by viable bacterial populations in protected reservoirs below the skin surface.
evidence: Inferred from the perturbation-recovery experiment data showing convergence to PMA-treated baseline shown in Figure 6C.

claim: After surface sterilization, the skin is repopulated by the same ASVs as were present before sterilization.
source: Examining repopulation dynamics more finely at the ASV level revealed that ASVs that were lost upon surface sterilization often reappeared over time, consistent with the model that surface repopulation can be driven by subsurface populations. Specifically, we found that after surface sterilization, the skin is repopulated by the same ASVs as were present before sterilization (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Qualitative analysis of ASV-level data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Bacteria thrive in protected areas below the skin surface and the DNA of their dead remains accumulates on the skin surface.
source: Together, these results suggest that bacteria thrive in protected areas below the skin surface and that the DNA of their dead remains accumulates on the skin surface.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of FISH, PMA-ddPCR, and perturbation-recovery experiments shown in Figures 1-6.

claim: The bacterial DNA on the skin surface acts as a fingerprint of the communities below.
source: In this way, the bacterial DNA on the skin surface acts as a fingerprint of the communities below.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that surface DNA composition reflects subsurface viable populations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The skin microbiome has a uniquely low fraction of viable bacteria compared to other human microbiome sites.
source: Furthermore, we show that the skin microbiome has a uniquely low fraction of viable bacteria compared to other human microbiome sites, indicating that most bacterial DNA on the skin surface is not associated with viable cells
evidence: Supported by PMA-ddPCR data comparing skin and non-skin microbiome sites shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A small number of bacterial families dominate each skin site.
source: Additionally, a small number of bacterial families dominate each skin site and traditional sequencing methods overestimate both the richness and diversity of the skin microbiome.
evidence: Supported by PMA-seq data showing low richness and dominance by few families shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Traditional sequencing methods overestimate both the richness and diversity of the skin microbiome.
source: Additionally, a small number of bacterial families dominate each skin site and traditional sequencing methods overestimate both the richness and diversity of the skin microbiome.
evidence: Supported by comparison of traditional sequencing and PMA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The skin microbiome is remarkably stable even in the wake of aggressive perturbation.
source: Bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that, while the skin microbiome is remarkably stable even in the wake of aggressive perturbation, repopulation of the skin surface is driven by the underlying viable population.
evidence: Supported by perturbation-recovery experiment data shown in Figure 6A showing stable composition.

claim: Repopulation of the skin surface is driven by the underlying viable population.
source: Bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed that, while the skin microbiome is remarkably stable even in the wake of aggressive perturbation, repopulation of the skin surface is driven by the underlying viable population.
evidence: Supported by perturbation-recovery experiment data showing convergence to PMA-treated baseline shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The skin microbiome affects immune system education.
source: For example, the human skin microbiome affects immune system education (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Polak-Witka et al., 2020), wound healing (Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017), colonization resistance (Byrd et al., 2018), modulation of gene expression in the skin (Meisel et al., 2018b), and may have a role in development (Meisel et al., 2018a).
evidence: Cited from Scharschmidt et al., 2015 and Polak-Witka et al., 2020.

claim: The skin microbiome affects wound healing.
source: For example, the human skin microbiome affects immune system education (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Polak-Witka et al., 2020), wound healing (Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017), colonization resistance (Byrd et al., 2018), modulation of gene expression in the skin (Meisel et al., 2018b), and may have a role in development (Meisel et al., 2018a).
evidence: Cited from Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017.

claim: The skin microbiome affects colonization resistance.
source: For example, the human skin microbiome affects immune system education (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Polak-Witka et al., 2020), wound healing (Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017), colonization resistance (Byrd et al., 2018), modulation of gene expression in the skin (Meisel et al., 2018b), and may have a role in development (Meisel et al., 2018a).
evidence: Cited from Byrd et al., 2018.

claim: The skin microbiome affects modulation of gene expression in the skin.
source: For example, the human skin microbiome affects immune system education (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Polak-Witka et al., 2020), wound healing (Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017), colonization resistance (Byrd et al., 2018), modulation of gene expression in the skin (Meisel et al., 2018b), and may have a role in development (Meisel et al., 2018a).
evidence: Cited from Meisel et al., 2018b.

claim: The skin microbiome may have a role in development.
source: For example, the human skin microbiome affects immune system education (Scharschmidt et al., 2015; Polak-Witka et al., 2020), wound healing (Kalan et al., 2019; Kim et al., 2019; Loesche et al., 2017), colonization resistance (Byrd et al., 2018), modulation of gene expression in the skin (Meisel et al., 2018b), and may have a role in development (Meisel et al., 2018a).
evidence: Cited from Meisel et al., 2018a with speculative language 'may have'.

claim: The skin is the largest organ in the human body, providing roughly 25 square meters for potential host–microbe interactions.
source: The skin is the largest organ in the human body, providing roughly 25 square meters for potential host–microbe interactions (Gallo, 2017).
evidence: Cited from Gallo, 2017.

claim: Human skin has the incredible ability to regenerate itself every 20–30 d.
source: It facilitates our tactile interactions with the world, separates us from the dangers of our daily lives, and has the incredible ability to regenerate itself every 20–30 d (Maeda, 2017).
evidence: Cited from Maeda, 2017.

claim: The skin microbiome is stable across months in longitudinal studies yet easily perturbed upon transient environmental changes like swimming.
source: Why is the skin microbiome stable across months in longitudinal studies yet easily perturbed upon transient environmental changes like swimming (Nielsen and Jiang, 2019)?
evidence: Cited from Nielsen and Jiang, 2019.

claim: Bacteria extend into deeper portions of the skin.
source: Additionally, while sequencing and culture-based studies have demonstrated that bacteria extend into deeper portions of the skin, the spatial distribution of the skin microbiome as a whole has not been well characterized (Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016; Lousada et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016; Lousada et al., 2021.

claim: The spatial distribution of the skin microbiome as a whole has not been well characterized.
source: Additionally, while sequencing and culture-based studies have demonstrated that bacteria extend into deeper portions of the skin, the spatial distribution of the skin microbiome as a whole has not been well characterized (Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016; Lousada et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about the state of the field with citations to Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Belkaid and Tamoutounour, 2016; Lousada et al., 2021.

claim: EUB338 is a universal bacterial fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) probe that hybridizes to bacterial 16S rRNA.
source: To address this gap, we determined the spatial distribution of bacterial cells in the skin using the universal bacterial fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) probe EUB338, which hybridizes to bacterial 16S rRNA (Amann et al., 1990).
evidence: Cited from Amann et al., 1990.

claim: Corynebacteria are readily cultured from nasal isolates.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that Corynebacteria are readily cultured from nasal isolates, which supports our PMA-seq finding that viable members of this taxon are abundant in the nares but not at most other skin sites (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from Liu et al., 2020.

claim: The key function of immune education by the skin microbiome occurs within hair follicles.
source: For example, our findings support previous work suggesting that the key function of immune education by the skin microbiome occurs within hair follicles (Polak-Witka et al., 2020), though cell-free DNA on the skin surface could also impact the immune system.
evidence: Cited from Polak-Witka et al., 2020 and inferred from the current study's findings.

claim: Cell-free DNA on the skin surface could impact the immune system.
source: For example, our findings support previous work suggesting that the key function of immune education by the skin microbiome occurs within hair follicles (Polak-Witka et al., 2020), though cell-free DNA on the skin surface could also impact the immune system.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential impact of cell-free DNA.

claim: Individual pores are colonized by clonal bacterial populations.
source: Our findings also support previous work showing that individual pores are colonized by clonal bacterial populations (Conwill et al., 2022).
evidence: Cited from Conwill et al., 2022.

claim: Stably colonizing the skin surface with exogenous bacteria has proved to be difficult and often requires abrasion.
source: Meanwhile, our results may help to explain why stably colonizing the skin surface with exogenous bacteria has proved to be difficult and often requires abrasion (Scharschmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from Scharschmidt et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of the stratum corneum (skin surface layers), which occurs during skin abrasion, may allow access to the deeper layers of tissue where the stable bacterial populations reside.
source: Disruption of the stratum corneum (skin surface layers), which occurs during skin abrasion, may allow access to the deeper layers of tissue where the stable bacterial populations reside.
evidence: Inferred from the current study's findings about subsurface bacterial populations.

claim: Targeting the bacteria within hair follicles may represent a better strategy for stably manipulating the skin microbiome or educating the immune system.
source: Thus, targeting the bacteria within hair follicles may represent a better strategy for stably manipulating the skin microbiome or educating the immune system.
evidence: Inferred from the current study's findings about viable bacteria in follicles.

claim: It has been known for some time that bacteria inhabit hair follicles.
source: While it has been known for some time that bacteria inhabit hair follicles (Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Lousada et al., 2021), our findings extend this knowledge and suggest that the viable bacteria of the skin microbiome are primarily restricted to these sites.
evidence: Cited from Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Lousada et al., 2021.

claim: The viable bacteria of the skin microbiome are primarily restricted to hair follicles and other cutaneous structures.
source: While it has been known for some time that bacteria inhabit hair follicles (Polak-Witka et al., 2020; Lousada et al., 2021), our findings extend this knowledge and suggest that the viable bacteria of the skin microbiome are primarily restricted to these sites.
evidence: Inferred from the combined FISH and PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 5.

claim: Bacteria can be readily cultured from the skin surface, but at far less abundance than suggested by the amount of bacterial DNA present on the skin.
source: This is further supported by our finding that bacteria can be readily cultured from the skin surface, but at far less abundance than suggested by the amount of bacterial DNA present on the skin.
evidence: Supported by CFU plating data compared to ddPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: The skin is primarily colonized by viable bacteria in pilosebaceous units and other skin invaginations.
source: The skin is primarily colonized by viable bacteria in pilosebaceous units and other skin invaginations, and the bacterial DNA on the skin surface is mostly from dead bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from the combined FISH and PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 5.

claim: Surface bacterial DNA could be easily washed away, while the viable subsurface bacteria remain unperturbed by washing, persisting as a small but stable source of new bacterial DNA that replenishes the skin surface over time.
source: We show that surface bacterial DNA could be easily washed away, while the viable subsurface bacteria remain unperturbed by washing, persisting as a small but stable source of new bacterial DNA that replenishes the skin surface over time.
evidence: Supported by perturbation-recovery experiment data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The life cycle of the skin microbiome may resemble the process of epithelial cell turnover in the skin.
source: Human skin cells are also born below the skin surface and are pushed to the surface as they die. In this way, the life cycle of the skin microbiome may resemble the process of epithelial cell turnover in the skin.
evidence: Speculative analogy based on the findings about bacterial distribution and turnover.

claim: The accessible DNA in non-skin microbiomes is generally representative of viable bacterial cells as all non-skin microbiomes tested had viability scores above 0.4.
source: The accessible DNA in non-skin microbiomes is generally representative of viable bacterial cells as all non-skin microbiomes tested had viability scores above 0.4.
evidence: Supported by PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Saliva contains many antimicrobial compounds.
source: Even saliva, which contains many antimicrobial compounds (van 't Hof et al., 2014), had a viability score nearly four times greater than the highest viability score for a skin microbiome.
evidence: Cited from van 't Hof et al., 2014.

claim: Saliva had a viability score nearly four times greater than the highest viability score for a skin microbiome.
source: Even saliva, which contains many antimicrobial compounds (van 't Hof et al., 2014), had a viability score nearly four times greater than the highest viability score for a skin microbiome.
evidence: Supported by PMA-ddPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The uniquely low viability score associated with the skin could be explained by passive mechanisms, like bacterial DNA adhering to the skin long after a bacterial cell dies.
source: The uniquely low viability score associated with the skin could be explained by passive mechanisms, like bacterial DNA adhering to the skin long after a bacterial cell dies.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed low viability scores.

claim: There could be active mechanisms like bacterial killing on the skin surface by factors like antimicrobial peptides produced by epithelial cells, competition between bacterial species, or exposure to harsh environmental factors such as starvation, UV radiation, or desiccation.
source: Alternatively, there could be active mechanisms like bacterial killing on the skin surface by factors like antimicrobial peptides produced by epithelial cells, competition between bacterial species, or exposure to harsh environmental factors such as starvation, UV radiation, or desiccation.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed low viability scores.

claim: Viable skin-associated bacteria are predominantly located in hair follicles and other cutaneous invaginations.
source: Here, we apply culturing, imaging, and molecular approaches to human and mouse skin samples, and find that the skin surface is colonized by fewer viable bacteria than predicted by bacterial DNA levels. Instead, viable skin-associated bacteria are predominantly located in hair follicles and other cutaneous invaginations.
evidence: Supported by FISH imaging data (Figures 1 and 5) and PMA-ddPCR data (Figure 2D).

claim: The skin surface is colonized by fewer viable bacteria than predicted by bacterial DNA levels.
source: Here, we apply culturing, imaging, and molecular approaches to human and mouse skin samples, and find that the skin surface is colonized by fewer viable bacteria than predicted by bacterial DNA levels.
evidence: Supported by PMA-ddPCR data (Figure 2C) and FISH imaging data (Figure 1).

claim: Most bacterial DNA on the skin surface is not associated with viable cells.
source: Furthermore, we show that the skin microbiome has a uniquely low fraction of viable bacteria compared to other human microbiome sites, indicating that most bacterial DNA on the skin surface is not associated with viable cells
evidence: Inferred from the low viability scores (0.02-0.12) measured by PMA-ddPCR shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Using PMA provides a much more accurate estimation of the viable skin microbiome.
source: Rather, our data indicate that the majority of the bacterial DNA on the skin surface are not within bacteria such that using PMA provides a much more accurate estimation of the viable skin microbiome.
evidence: Supported by comparison of PMA-ddPCR to CFU data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: Traditional 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing does not differentiate between DNA originating from live or dead cells.
source: The inability of 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to differentiate between these two types of bacterial populations has been mentioned as a potential downfall of the method (Byrd et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Byrd et al., 2018 and established knowledge about sequencing methods.

claim: An independent analysis of glabella samples from five healthy volunteers including contamination controls revealed the same trends that traditional sequencing overrepresented both diversity and richness with or without contaminant removal.
source: An independent analysis of glabella samples from five healthy volunteers including contamination controls revealed the same trends that traditional sequencing overrepresented both diversity and richness with or without contaminant removal (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: C. acnes has been shown by traditional sequencing to comprise upwards of 50% of the skin microbiome irrespective of site type.
source: The family Propionibacteriaceae includes a major component of the skin microbiome, C. acnes, which has been shown by traditional sequencing to comprise upwards of 50% of the skin microbiome irrespective of site type (Byrd et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from Byrd et al., 2018.

claim: The significant numbers of bacteria observed in hair follicles suggest that the absence of surface bacteria is not merely due to the relatively clean conditions in which laboratory mice are housed.
source: The significant numbers of bacteria observed in hair follicles suggest that the absence of surface bacteria is not merely due to the relatively clean conditions in which laboratory mice are housed.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of abundant follicular bacteria in laboratory mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: FISH staining can be used to reliably visualize bacteria on the skin surface.
source: FISH staining revealed many bacteria on the surface of these samples, confirming that this technique can be used to reliably visualize bacteria on the skin surface (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by positive control experiment with E. coli applied to mouse skin shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A probe encoding the reverse complement of the EUB338 FISH probe (NONEUB338) did not significantly hybridize to the skin surface or follicles.
source: As a negative control, we also confirmed that a probe encoding the reverse complement of the EUB338 FISH probe (NONEUB338) did not significantly hybridize to the skin surface or follicles (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by negative control experiment shown in Figure 5C.
